Before choosing an option, identify the exact definition or theorem the question is testing. Parse every displayed expression literally, then compare the options’ hypotheses, quantifiers, exponents, endpoint spaces, and requested level of detail. Do not invent a theorem, exceptional case, or stronger conclusion from analogy or from a plausible-sounding citation. If you cannot verify a stronger claim, select only what the stated result supports.

Prevent regression by retaining these exact distinctions: for ℓ1(Γ), semiprojectivity holds for every Γ, while 1+-projectivity holds iff Γ is countable; for the annuity model, derive the ruin-tail exponent rather than assuming it is the symbol γ (the stated asymptotic has exponent 1−γ); for the hypercube variation question, preserve the established qualitative unboundedness for every finite r and do not promote an illustrative example to a quantitative theorem without checking every quantifier and constant; and for the homogenization estimate, a bound valid for all t may have a time-dependent right-hand side—do not replace the logarithm involving max(t, ε)/ε with a time-independent ε|log ε| claim. Under the stated local-mass conditions in the PDE problem, use the theorem’s finite-time blow-up conclusion rather than a generic global-existence heuristic.

For specialized identities, preserve the input’s exact structure: in A_f(1,n), keep the square on the argument a_f((n/d²)²); for the Dyck-path statistic, count non-origin anchors as defined and do not add 1 to the denominator merely to avoid a perceived zero; and for the MZV identity, write out the ordered blocks before matching options—the placement of the a, b, and c blocks is decisive. Reduce congruences using the given parameter ranges, but do not let apparently redundant choices tempt you into changing the theorem’s condition.

Do not infer unstated strength from nearby concepts. The limiting-period result gives containment in the specified algebra; do not upgrade it to finite generation without support. For the Brauer-Manin conclusion, use the stated point-separation condition rather than treating finiteness or generic injectivity as interchangeable. For the pencil-of-quadrics question, assert the invariant rational map only; do not add unproved fiber-orbit or codimension claims. For the Bowman construction, distinguish its topology from the original topology and give the explicit-metric conclusion when that is what is asked. For minimal embeddings, never assume every minimal hypersurface of a sphere is totally geodesic; check standard product examples and the claimed ambient dimension before rejecting an existence statement. For KdV, distinguish C((0,T); H^s) from C([0,T]; H^s) and follow the theorem’s endpoint statement even when compatibility conditions are mentioned.

Use examples as checks, not as substitutes for the general result. Keep the exact algebraic derivations and complete classifications that have been consistently successful, and stop once the option is verified; do not reopen a settled conclusion with unsupported speculation.
